citations.quote:
Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

derivations.claim: Integer induction gives $2^n\ge n+1$ for $n\ge0$: the initial equality is immediate and $2^{n+1}\ge2(n+1)\ge n+2$. For $t>0$, [F1] supplies a natural $N>\max(t,1/t,1)$, so $2^{-N}<t<2^N$. The finite set of integers $j\in[-N,N]$ with $2^j\le t$ is nonempty and has a largest element $E$; it satisfies $2^E\le t<2^{E+1}$. Strict increase of powers of two makes $E$ unique. Thus the stated $E(x)$ exists for every $x\ne0$. In its binade, the finitely many points $m2^{E-p+1}$, $2^{p-1}\le m\le2^p$, bracket $t$; their adjacent neighbors determine its nearest point. Points outside that bracket cannot be nearer, and zero is farther than a positive grid point; negative arguments follow by reflection. On a binade $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$, the nonnegative grid has spacing $2^{j-p+1}$. Its consecutive midpoints partition the real line into nearest-point cells, proving monotonicity and exactness on the grid; reflection preserves the even-significand tie rule, proving oddness. Every nonzero real number has two bracketing grid points, so a nearest point exists and is nonzero for a nonzero argument. The gaps on either side of a grid point $c\ne0$ are at most $q(c)$, including the half-sized lower gap at a power of two. Its rounding cell therefore gives $|R(t)-t|\le q(R(t))/2$. Also, for any power of two $h$, every integer multiple $nh$ with $|n|\le2^p$ is in $\mathbb B_p$: the integer has at most $p$ significant bits, except $|n|=2^p$, which is a power of two.

Suppose $x,y\ne0$ and $|x|\ge|y|$, and put $h=q(y)$. Both operands and their exact sum $t=x+y$ are integer multiples of $h$. Whenever $|t|\le|y|$, step 1.1 makes $t$ representable because $|y|<2^p h$. In particular, if $|R(t)|<|y|$, monotonicity and the fixed grid points $\pm|y|$ imply $|t|<|y|$, so $R(t)=t$. Otherwise $|R(t)|\ge|y|$, hence its binade spacing is an integer multiple of $h$, so $\rho=R(t)-t$ is an integer multiple of $h$. Since $x$ and $y$ themselves are candidate nearest points, $|\rho|\le\min(|t-x|,|t-y|)=|y|<2^p h$; step 1.1 makes $\rho$ representable. The zero-operand cases have $\rho=0$, and interchange handles the other magnitude order. This proves the second assertion, including the strict small-rounded-sum case.

For the subtraction assertion, change both signs and interchange operands so that $x\ge y>0$ and $x\le2y$. Then $0\le x-y\le y$, and the grid argument in step 1.2, applied to $x$ and $-y$, shows that $x-y$ is representable. Reversing the transformations proves all same-sign cases; zero gives only the trivial zero pair.

For the ordered transform, if $A=0$ then $B=0$ and all outputs vanish. Otherwise oddness allows $A>0$. Since $0\le A+B\le2A$ and $2A$ is representable, monotonicity gives $0\le S\le2A$. If $B\ge-A/2$, it also gives $S\ge A/2$; step 1.3 then makes $S-A$ exact. If $B<-A/2$, the operands $A$ and $-B$ meet step 1.3, so $S=A+B$ exactly and $S-A=B$ is exact as well. Thus always $Z=S-A=B+\rho$, where $\rho=S-(A+B)$. Step 1.2 makes $-\rho$ representable, so $T=R(B-Z)=-\rho=A+B-S$ exactly.

citations.quote: For real floating-point a,b compute s=fl(a+b), z=fl(s-a), e=fl((a-(s-z))+(b-z)), with every operation separately rounded. Return the first range failure and operation index if an exact intermediate is nonzero subnormal, overflowed, or otherwise invalid; otherwise return (s,e). The fixed sequence terminates. Its general exact-transform claim is a separate theorem; this definition alone does not prove exact recovery.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

For an integer $p\ge2$, let $\mathbb B_p=\{0\}\cup\{\pm m2^k: m,k\in\mathbb Z,\ 2^{p-1}\le m<2^p\}$, with unbounded exponent. Let $R$ round a real number to its nearest member of $\mathbb B_p$, breaking ties by the even normalized significand; set $R(0)=0$. For $x\ne0$ put $E(x)$ be the unique integer with $2^{E(x)}\le|x|<2^{E(x)+1}$, and set $q(x)=2^{E(x)-p+1}$. The following hold.

- $R$ is monotone, odd, and fixes $\mathbb B_p$. For $R(t)\ne0$, $|R(t)-t|\le q(R(t))/2$.
- If $x,y\in\mathbb B_p$, then $\rho=R(x+y)-(x+y)$ belongs to $\mathbb B_p$ and $|\rho|\le\min(|x|,|y|)$. If $|R(x+y)|<\min(|x|,|y|)$, the sum is exact.
- If $x,y\in\mathbb B_p$ have the same sign and $|x|/2\le|y|\le2|x|$, then $x-y\in\mathbb B_p$ (Sterbenz exact subtraction).
- If $A,B\in\mathbb B_p$ and $|A|\ge|B|$, then $S=R(A+B)$, $Z=R(S-A)$, $T=R(B-Z)$ satisfy $Z=S-A$ and $T=A+B-S$ exactly.

derivations.claim: Let $R$ denote unbounded binary nearest-even rounding from [F3]. On the closed normal range, bounded-format rounding equals $R$: the normal grid is identical, its endpoints are representable, and a point beyond either endpoint cannot beat that endpoint for an exact argument inside the range. Additional subnormal values cannot alter a nearest choice there. At a boundary power of two the normalized even significand gives the same tie choice; zero is exact. All inputs belong to $\mathbb B_p$. By [F2], induction over the six operations [F1] therefore identifies the actual successful computation with the same sequence using $R$. It suffices to prove its unbounded identity.
Put $\rho=s-(a+b)$. If $|a|\ge|b|$, the ordered transform [F3] gives $z=s-a$ and $R(b-z)=-\rho$ exactly. Consequently $v=R(s-z)=a$, $w=0$, $t=-\rho$, and $e=-\rho$. This includes $a=b=0$.

Suppose $|a|<|b|$. If $|s|<|a|$, the small-rounded-sum assertion [F3] makes $s=a+b$ exact. Then $z=b$, $v=a$, $w=t=e=0$ and $\rho=0$. For the remaining case $|s|\ge|a|$, apply the ordered transform to $(s,-a)$: it says $R(z-s)=z-s$ and $R(-a-(z-s))=(s-a)-z$. Oddness therefore gives $v=R(s-z)=s-z$ and $w=R(a-v)=z-(s-a)$ exactly. Writing $\sigma=z-(s-a)$, we have $w=\sigma$ and $z=b+\rho+\sigma$.

In this remaining case, oddness permits simultaneous sign reversal so that $b>0$. Since $|a|<b$, we have $0<a+b<2b$, and monotonicity gives $0<s\le2b$. Thus $q(s)\le q(2b)=2q(b)$ and the rounding bound yields $|\rho|\le q(b)\le b/2$, since $p\ge2$. Also $|\rho|\le|a|<b$ by the addition-error bound. Therefore $b/2\le s-a=b+\rho<2b$; monotonicity, fixing $b/2$ and $2b$, gives $b/2\le z\le2b$. Sterbenz [F3] makes $t=R(b-z)=b-z=-\rho-\sigma$ exact. Finally $w+t=-\rho$ is representable by the addition-error assertion [F3], so $e=R(w+t)=-\rho$ exactly. Oddness gives the same conclusion before sign reversal.

The branches in steps 1.2, 2.1, and 2.2 cover every magnitude order and sign, and each gives $e=-\rho=(a+b)-s$. Step 1.1 transfers this identity to every successful finite-range call, proving $s+e=a+b$. A nonzero subnormal exact intermediate or overflow returns failure under [F2] and is outside the success conclusion; no extra hidden range assumption is used in any successful boundary case.

$$s=\operatorname{fl}(a+b),\qquad e=(a+b)-s,\qquad s+e=a+b$$
exactly in real arithmetic. No ordering or sign condition on the inputs is required; zeros, exact cancellation, and all successful calls at either normal-range boundary are included.

routine_steps.claim: The spacing above $1$ is $2^{-52}$, so $1+2^{-53}$ is the midpoint between $1$ and $1+2^{-52}$. The even-significand endpoint is $1$; hence $s=1$. The next exact operands give $z=1-1=0$, $v=1-0=1$, $w=1-1=0$, and $t=2^{-53}-0=2^{-53}$. Each is representable, so each subtraction is exact.

The final exact intermediate is $w+t=2^{-53}$, hence $e=2^{-53}$. The first exact sum $1+2^{-53}$ and every later nonzero exact intermediate ($1$ or $2^{-53}$) are normal and within range; the zero intermediates are allowed by [F3]. Thus the call succeeds, its format satisfies [F2], and $s+e=1+2^{-53}=a+b$ exactly, also directly verified by these outputs.
